## The Last Holy Week: Chronicle of a Fading Peal

Holy Week 2025 in Almuñécar was not measured by the number of processional floats or the influx of visitors, but by the physical capacity of three men to climb spiral staircases. The three bell ringers who still practice the craft in this town in the province of Granada took turns during those days with the precision of a military relay, aware that any forced absence would force the brotherhoods to press a button. And the button, although it reproduces the sound, does not reproduce the intention.

The first shift began on Viernes de Dolores, when the brotherhood of the Nazareno required the vespers toll. One of the bell ringers, over seventy years old and suffering from osteoarthritis that deforms his knuckles, climbed the forty-three steps of the tower of the Encarnación, supporting himself against the whitewashed wall. The effort cost him a pause of several minutes before he could grasp the clapper, but the peal rang out clear, with that broken cadence that the locals recognize as the announcement of a procession. Down below, in the square, the elderly looked up at the first toll, like someone recognizing the voice of a family member on the other end of the phone.

Jueves Santo marked the first breaking point. The brotherhood of the Santísimo Cristo de la Expiración had scheduled its procession for nine o'clock at night, but the bell ringer in charge of that shift suffered a bout of vertigo at midday. His family forced him to rest, and the brotherhood found itself with an uncomfortable dilemma: either suspend the manual ringing or activate the automatic mechanism installed in the parish. They opted for the latter. The result was a metallic, regular, soulless peal, which some locals later described as "the sound of a washing machine on the spin cycle." Criticism was not long in coming, especially from the older residents, who interpreted that toll as a lack of respect for tradition and for the titular image itself.

Viernes Santo dawned with palpable tension in the streets of the old town. The other two bell ringers, aware of what had happened the night before, decided to divide the stations of penitence with no margin for unforeseen events. One of them, the youngest of the group at sixty-four, committed to covering the morning and afternoon tolls, while the third, with a hip that had been operated on twice, reserved himself for the grand procession of the night. The coordination worked, but the physical toll was high: at the end of the day, both men had to be assisted in descending the towers, with trembling legs and gasping for breath.

Sábado Santo was experienced as a tense truce. The brotherhoods, gathered in an emergency meeting in the sacristy of the Encarnación, debated the advisability of resorting to automatic ringing for the remaining processions so as not to subject the bell ringers to excessive strain. The discussion pitted two positions against each other: those who defended the preservation of manual ringing at all costs, and those who prioritized the health of the three men. There was no formal agreement, but an intermediate solution prevailed: the bell ringers would only ring for the essential moments—the departure, the passing through the main square, and the return—and the rest of the route would be left in silence or accompanied by the bands.

On Domingo de Resurrección, the Procession of the Encuentro put the final touch to an exhausting week. The oldest bell ringer, the one who had suffered the bout of vertigo on Jueves Santo, insisted on climbing the tower for the peal of glory. He did so accompanied by his granddaughter, a teenager who supported him by the arm during the ascent and who witnessed, for the first time, her grandfather's complete ritual: checking the ropes, adjusting the clapper, leaning his body to put force into the first strike. The peal rang out like a victory, but also like a farewell. No one said it out loud, though everyone thought it: that could be the last Domingo de Resurrección with a fully manual peal in Almuñécar.

The figures from that week summarize the fragility of the craft. Of the fourteen planned processional tolls, only nine were executed manually. The remaining five were resolved with the automatic system or simply suppressed. The brotherhoods, which for decades had taken the availability of the bell ringers for granted, suddenly discovered the precariousness of a tradition that depends on three aging bodies and a will that is running out. The older neighbors, heirs to a language of sound that is no longer taught, expressed their discontent in the huddles of the square and at the doors of the churches, with that mixture of resignation and reproach that characterizes those who see a world disappearing without anyone consulting them.

Holy Week 2025 was not, strictly speaking, the end of manual ringing in Almuñécar. The three bell ringers are still alive and, as far as their strength allows, willing to repeat the experience next year. But it was the first time that automation crept into the heart of the processions, not as a theoretical threat but as a practical necessity. And that, in a craft transmitted through imitation and direct contact with the rope, amounts to a silent surrender. The question left hanging in the air after the last toll of Domingo de Resurrección was not whether the bell ringers could endure another Holy Week, but whether anyone would be there to take up the clapper when they can no longer climb the stairs.
